title: Class attributes, instance attributes, and shadowing
sources: Python 3.14 Tutorial, chapter 9 Classes: class and instance variables; Python 3.14 Data Model: custom classes and instances; reviewed 2026-10-03
masterChecklist: Classes, instances, methods, self, constructors, attributes, class versus instance variables
whyItMatters: A configuration value shared across every learner is different from progress that belongs to one learner. Confusing the two can leak state between users or make updates appear inconsistent.
simpleExplanation: A class attribute belongs to the class and can be found through its instances. An instance attribute belongs to one object. For ordinary attributes, a read such as mina.label checks Mina's instance first and then looks to her class; assigning mina.label = ... stores a value on Mina and hides the class value for Mina only. This is called shadowing. Changing Learner.label later affects instances that have not shadowed it. A mutable class attribute such as a list is especially dangerous for per-user data because all instances may mutate the same list. Descriptor-backed attributes such as properties have additional lookup rules, covered in a later lesson.
mentalModel: The class owns a shared noticeboard; each instance owns its own notebook. A notebook entry with the same name hides what that notebook would have read from the noticeboard.
outcomes: Distinguish class-wide defaults from per-instance data.
Predict what happens when an instance shadows a class attribute.
Avoid a shared mutable list for independent learners.
Use vars(instance) to inspect the instance's own ordinary attributes.

realWorldExample.scenario: A progress app has a class-wide display label and separate completed lessons for each learner.
realWorldExample.riskWithoutSetup: Putting completed = [] on the class means one learner's additions can appear in another learner's record.
realWorldExample.professionalApproach: Keep a simple shared default label on the class; put each learner's completed list in __init__ and test two instances.

workedExample.code:
class Learner:
    label = 'member'  # Shared default, not per-user progress.

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.completed = []

mina = Learner('Mina')
leo = Learner('Leo')
print(mina.label, leo.label)
mina.label = 'mentor'  # Shadows the class value for Mina only.
mina.completed.append('loops')
print(mina.label, leo.label)
print(mina.completed, leo.completed)
print('label' in vars(mina), 'label' in vars(leo))
explanation: Before shadowing, both objects read Learner.label.
mina.label = 'mentor' adds an instance attribute; Leo still reads the class default.
The completed lists came from separate __init__ calls, so only Mina's progress changes.
vars(instance) shows the ordinary instance namespace in this example; it is not a universal introspection API for objects without __dict__.
workedExample.expectedOutput:
member member
mentor member
['loops'] []
True False
workedExample.safeExperiment: After shadowing Mina's label, set Learner.label = 'student'. Predict Mina's and Leo's labels before running.

procedure: Decide whether a value is shared configuration or individual object state.
Put immutable shared defaults on the class and individual mutable data in __init__.
Create two instances and mutate only one.
Test reading a class default, then shadowing it on one instance.
Inspect vars(instance) for ordinary instance attributes, while remembering some objects use slots or descriptors.

commonMistakes.mistake: Declaring completed = [] in the class body for per-user progress.
commonMistakes.why: Every instance can mutate the same list.
commonMistakes.avoid: Create self.completed = [] for each new instance.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming mina.label = ... changes Learner.label for everyone.
commonMistakes.why: Ordinary assignment on mina creates or replaces her instance attribute.
commonMistakes.avoid: Update the class explicitly only when a truly class-wide default should change.

commonMistakes.why: Some objects lack an instance __dict__, such as slotted objects.
commonMistakes.avoid: Use vars only when an instance dictionary exists; use the documented public interface otherwise.

lab.solution:
class Learner:
    label = 'member'

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.completed = []

mina = Learner('Mina')
leo = Learner('Leo')
mina.label = 'mentor'
mina.completed.append('loops')
print(mina.label, leo.label)
print(mina.completed, leo.completed)
print('label' in vars(mina), 'label' in vars(leo))
lab.solutionExplanation: Mina shadows only her label, while both progress lists are independent instance state.

projectConnection.milestone: Use a shared display default without sharing each learner's progress list.
projectConnection.definitionOfDone: Tests demonstrate two independent lists, a single-instance label override, and no accidental cross-learner change.

assessment.question: Where should a learner's mutable completed list be created?
assessment.explanation: That gives each instance its own list.

assessment.question: What happens after mina.label = 'mentor' when Learner.label is 'member'?
assessment.answer: Mina reads mentor; other instances without an override still read member.
assessment.explanation: Mina's ordinary instance attribute shadows the class attribute.

assessment.question: Does vars(instance) work for every Python object?
assessment.answer: No; it requires an instance dictionary.
assessment.explanation: Slotted and some built-in objects may not expose one.
